blocks.source: Vol III, KV Cache Management, § Historical Perspective and Further Reading
blocks.md: Almost every memory management technique in this chapter resolves an architectural problem that time-sharing operating systems encountered decades ago. When early programs outgrew physical core memory, the Manchester Atlas one-level store introduced paging. An address translation table mapped a program's contiguous virtual address space onto scattered physical page frames, freeing programmers from managing manual overlays and allowing memory to allocate without contiguous physical reservations. Decoupling virtual addresses from physical layout promptly exposed new systems trade-offs.

questions.q: The section **Historical Perspective and Further Reading** develops one of the chapter's claims. Which one?
options: Fixed-size blocks mapped by a per-sequence block table remove the stranded memory of full-cap reservation and bound tail waste below one block.

A content-keyed radix tree finds the longest retained common prefix, leaf-first eviction keeps residency prefix-closed, and efficacy is the token-weighted hit rate after availability, permission, and block rounding.

By Little's law a fixed pool of slots sustains a turn rate inversely proportional to residence, so holding state through a synchronous tool wait divides the memory-bound turn rate by 1 + T_tool/T_model.
During a tool wait the engine keeps, moves, or drops only uniquely reclaimable blocks, and offloading pays only when the wait exceeds the transfer round trip and memory is contested.
